parts.title: Mice Vaccinated with the Outer-Coat Proteins VP2 or VP5 of Bluetongue Virus Show Worse Signs of Illness and More Deaths After Infection with a Weakened, Different Type of the Virus
parts.abstract:
Bluetongue is a disease of cattle, sheep and other ruminants, both on farms and in the wild, and it costs farmers a great deal of money. It is caused by bluetongue virus (BTV). The virus comes in at least 36 different types, called serotypes. Which type a virus is depends on one of its outer-coat proteins, called VP2. Most of these types are spread by tiny biting insects called Culicoides midges.

We used a special kind of mouse called IFNAR(−/−) mice. Their immune system cannot make interferon, a chemical signal that helps the body fight viruses. We vaccinated the mice with VP2 proteins from BTV types 1, 4 or 8, or with a smaller outer-coat protein called VP5 from BTV type 10. These proteins were made in plants, so we call them rVP2 and rVP5. Some mice were given a harmless salt solution (PBS) instead, as a comparison group. Later, we infected the mice with one of three viruses. Two were strong, disease-causing strains of BTV type 4 or type 8. The third was a weakened, harmless version of BTV type 1, called BTV-1RGC7.

Mice vaccinated with rVP2 were protected against the same type of virus they had been vaccinated with. They had less virus in their blood, which we measured with a test called qRT-PCR. They also had milder signs of illness and fewer deaths. We saw no protection against other types of the virus.

However, when the mice were infected with the weakened BTV-1, the picture changed. Mice vaccinated with rVP2 from BTV-4 or BTV-8, or with rVP5 from BTV-10, all had worse signs of illness, more virus in their blood and more deaths.

We discuss one possible explanation. Some antibodies stick to the outer-coat proteins of these different virus types but do not stop the virus from infecting cells. These are called non-neutralising antibodies. Because the outer-coat proteins of the different types are related, such antibodies could lead to 'antibody-dependent enhancement of infection' (ADE). In ADE, antibodies that do not block infection actually help the virus get into the body's cells. Interactions like this could affect how different BTV strains spread and appear in the wild. That would matter when planning and carrying out vaccination campaigns.
parts.introduction_first: Antibodies are proteins the immune system makes to recognise and attack a particular germ. A virus can be stopped, or 'neutralised', when antibodies attach to certain spots on the proteins that help it attach to cells. These spots are called neutralisation epitopes. When antibodies cover them, the virus cannot latch onto the matching spots on the animal's cells, so infection cannot start. The virus also cannot multiply afterwards [1]. Not every antibody that sticks to the virus surface stops it. Even antibodies that do not neutralise can make virus particles clump together. The immune system's cells can then clear these clumps away.
parts.conclusion:
5. Conclusions

In ruminants in the wild, the severity of signs of illness and the amount of BTV in the blood could be affected by processes like ADE. These processes may matter after vaccination campaigns that use vaccines against a single virus type. This is especially true if the vaccines are mainly based on the VP2 and VP5 proteins. Such vaccines could help weakened BTV vaccine strains that have been used in the wild before to stay in the body for longer [31,53,54].

Inactivated vaccines, which contain killed virus, have been used widely, particularly in Europe. This has inevitably left many animals with antibodies against BTV that would be unlikely to stop other types of the virus. However, processes like ADE could make later outbreaks caused by these other viruses more severe, or help them spread. They might also help explain why BTV-6 and BTV-11 vaccine strains have been found in Europe [31,54].

Which types of the virus cause outbreaks one after another in areas where the disease is always present could depend on each animal's past infections. Those infections shape which antibodies the animal or the population carries. The effect depends on how closely the outer-coat proteins of the different types involved match. More studies in mice, sheep and cattle are needed. They should find out how much the matching of BTV types matters, and what kind of ADE processes, if any, are involved.

BTV belongs to a group of viruses called orbiviruses. These viruses have similar shapes, multiply in similar ways and spread in similar ways. So any ADE process that affects BTV could also affect other orbiviruses. It may even matter for other viruses that come in many types and carry their genetic material as RNA.

Our results confirm that VP2 proteins, and the antibodies the body makes against them, protect against the same type of BTV. They also show that VP2 proteins made in plants could be used as ingredients in vaccines made from separate protein pieces. However, the results also show that it is important to think about ADE when planning vaccination campaigns with vaccines against a single type of the virus, whether those vaccines are inactivated or made from protein pieces.

To prevent problems that ADE could cause, vaccines should include ingredients that trigger protection against many types of the virus. One example is the immune system's T cells, which can recognise and destroy infected cells. T cells can be triggered by BTV proteins that are not part of the outer coat, called NS1 and NS2, or by the inner protein VP7. These proteins change less from one type of the virus to another, and they trigger protective T-cell responses that work across different types [2,55].
parts.introduction_rest:
Vaccines against viruses are medicines given before an infection, to protect the person or animal who receives them. They aim to protect them fully or partly against catching the virus, against serious signs of illness, or both. Most vaccines do this in one of two ways. They make the body produce neutralising antibodies, which stop the virus from infecting cells. Or they encourage T cells, which can destroy cells that do become infected. Some vaccines trigger protection through the immune system's cells instead of through antibodies. This kind of protection is called cell-mediated immunity, and it is an important part of the protection the body builds up after meeting a germ. Most vaccines that do this use a 'viral vector'. This is a harmless virus that carries the instructions for one particular protein of the germ into the body's cells, so that the cells make that protein themselves [2,3].

Most vaccines approved to prevent diseases caused by germs (parasites, bacteria or viruses) work by triggering a protective antibody response [4]. However, this does not always work as hoped. Some viruses come in many types. An animal that has antibodies against just one type, whether it caught the virus or was vaccinated against it, can show different, or even more severe, signs of illness after it catches a different type [5,6]. The processes behind this are known together as 'antibody-dependent enhancement of infection' (ADE). They are seen mainly in infections by viruses that carry their genetic material as RNA and come in many types.

One way ADE can happen is that antibodies make the virus more able to infect cells [7]. The part of an antibody that sticks to the virus is called the Fc region. When this part is attached to the virus, it can grab onto matching spots, called Fc receptors, on the surface of macrophages. Macrophages are large immune cells that swallow germs. This helps the virus get inside them and makes it more able to infect these cells. This has been seen in infections with dengue virus (DENV) and with feline infectious peritonitis virus (FIPV), a virus that causes a serious illness in cats [5,6,8]. For this kind of ADE to happen, the virus must be able to infect macrophages and other cells with Fc receptors in the reticuloendothelial system. This is the body's network of cells that swallow germs and clear them from the blood and tissues.

ADE can also happen in a different way. Antibodies that do not stop infection can stick to the surface of virus particles. This can make too many clumps of virus and antibody form. These clumps can damage the body's own cells, or set off chains of cytokines, which are chemical signals that immune cells use to call up inflammation [9,10,11]. The clumps and the cytokines can draw more immune cells to the area and switch on the complement system, a group of proteins that attack germs. This kind of boost to the immune response is best known in infections by viruses that attack the airways. There it leads to enhanced respiratory disease, meaning a worse illness of the airways and lungs. Viruses that can cause this include respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and measles virus, especially in people who were vaccinated earlier with vaccines made from killed virus [9,12,13,14,15]. ADE and enhanced respiratory disease have been seen in infections with both SARS-CoV (the virus that causes SARS) and MERS-CoV (the virus that causes MERS), both in laboratory tests and in living animals [9]. For COVID-19, it has been suggested that the damage to the body is likely caused by the formation of clumps, the build-up of complement proteins and the local switching-on of the immune system [9].

Many orbiviruses come in several types. These include bluetongue virus (BTV), epizootic haemorrhagic disease virus (EHDV) and African horse sickness virus (AHSV). Which type an orbivirus is depends on how its cell-attaching protein, the major outer-coat protein (OC1), fits with neutralising antibodies. This can be tested in neutralisation tests, which check whether antibodies can stop the virus from infecting cells [16]. In orbiviruses spread by midges, which includes BTV, the type of the virus is set by the order of the building blocks (amino acids) in the larger outer-coat protein VP2 (OC1) [17]. There are currently more than 36 recognised types of BTV. We speculate that this could lead to ADE in areas where several types are circulating. The orbivirus outer coat also contains a second protein, VP5 (OC2). This protein helps the virus push through the cell's outer membrane when infection starts [18]. The VP5 of BTV may help decide which type the virus is [19,20,21,22], possibly by interacting with VP2. However, it does not appear to bind neutralising antibodies [23].

A ruminant usually catches BTV for the first time through the bite of an infected adult Culicoides midge [24]. After that, immune cells called dendritic cells and macrophages carry infectious BTV particles from the skin to the lymph nodes, the small glands where immune cells gather. The virus multiplies there and is then carried to other organs [25,26,27]. As it multiplies in macrophages and in the cells that line blood vessels, the virus makes the body produce and release more cytokines and other substances that affect blood vessels. This raises the fever in infected ruminants [26]. It can damage blood vessels, so that fluid leaks out of them and there are bleeds in many tissues, including the lungs. This adds to breathing illness, which is a common sign of severe BTV infections [10,11,27].

The amount of virus in the blood of an infected animal shows how much BTV is multiplying and how much of it is being released into the blood and circulating. But it does not always match up in a fixed way with how severe the signs of illness are. Cattle infected with BTV often show few signs of illness, yet they often have more virus in their blood than infected sheep, which often show more severe signs of illness [28]. In sheep and cattle, BTV can also stay in the blood for a long time after infection, even after the signs of illness have gone [29,30]. However, a quick rise in the amount of virus in the blood soon after infection may be an early sign of how severe the illness will be in that animal.

We have been studying how BTV infections develop and how they can be controlled. To do this, we have used outer-coat proteins made in plants and strong, disease-causing strains of BTV types 1, 4 and 8. These strains have caused recent outbreaks of the disease in Europe and have been used in the vaccination programmes linked to them [10,27,31]. In earlier studies, we showed that the VP2 proteins made in plants from BTV-4 and BTV-8 (as described here) raised antibodies in IFNAR(−/−) mice and in rabbits. These antibodies recognised the matching VP2 proteins and viruses, in both ELISA tests (a lab test that measures antibodies) and serum neutralisation tests (tests that check whether antibodies in the blood can stop the virus) [32,33].

The immune responses in the mice also protected them against a deadly dose of the matching type of virus, but not of a different type. After infection with the different type, some of the mice had more virus in their blood early on than the mice that had not been vaccinated. This suggests a response of the ADE type. However, all of the unprotected mice died within 3 to 5 days after infection. These were the mice that had not been vaccinated, and the mice vaccinated with the VP2 of the different type. They died too soon for us to fully check whether they had worse signs of illness [32].

In this follow-up study, we used strong, disease-causing strains of BTV-4 and BTV-8, as well as a weakened, harmless strain of BTV-1, to infect IFNAR(−/−) mice. This confirmed that vaccinating with VP2 proteins made in plants protects against the matching type of virus. Because the mice survived longer after infection with the weakened BTV-1, we also had the chance to look for any worse signs of illness, or deaths, in animals that had been vaccinated with the VP2 or VP5 proteins of other types.
parts.methods:
2. Materials and Methods

2.1. Ethics Statement

We vaccinated the animals following the European Union's animal welfare law (Directive 2010/63/EU). The Ethics Committee for animal experimentation of Anses-EnvA-UPEC approved our plans for the experiment (project licence Number: 19-028).

2.2. Growing Cells and Viruses

We grew two kinds of cells in the laboratory. The first was a line of baby hamster kidney cells called BSR cells. They are a clone of an older line called BHK-21 cells [34]. We kept them at 37 °C in a nutrient liquid called Dulbecco's modified Eagle medium (DMEM). To this we added 10% foetal bovine serum, a rich animal blood product that helps cells grow, and 100 IU of penicillin and 100 µg of streptomycin per ml, which are antibiotics that stop bacteria. The cells were kept in air containing 5% carbon dioxide (CO2). The second kind was a line of cells from the midge Culicoides sonorensis, called KC cells. We grew these at 28 °C in Schneider's insect medium, with the same serum and antibiotics added.

We made the weakened BTV-1 vaccine strain, BTV-1RGC7, using a method called reverse genetics, as described in an earlier paper [35]. In reverse genetics, scientists start from the virus's full set of genetic instructions, called its genome, and use it to build a new virus. We based ours on the genome of the reference strain BTV-1RSArrrr/01. This reference strain is available online (https://www.reoviridae.org/dsRNA_virus_proteins/ReoID/btv-1.htm#RSArrrr/01, accessed on 19 December 2020). The weakened BTV-1RGC7 can infect IFNAR(−/−) mice, but it causes only mild signs of illness, and the mice then recover fully [35].

We also used two strong strains of the virus, BTV-4RSArrrr/04 and BTV8RSArrrr/08. Both are available online (BTV-4: https://www.reoviridae.org/dsRNA_virus_proteins/ReoID/btv-4.htm#RSArrrr/04; BTV-8: https://www.reoviridae.org/dsRNA_virus_proteins/ReoID/btv-8.htm#RSArrrr/08, both accessed on 19 December 2020). We obtained them from the orbivirus reference collection at the Pirbright Institute in the UK.

2.3. Infecting Cells and Cleaning Up the Virus Before Injecting It into IFNAR(−/−) Mice

We infected a single layer of BSR cells, covering 85% of the surface, with BTV-1RGC7 or with the reference strains of BTV-4 or BTV-8. We used 0.05 pfu of virus for each cell. The pfu, or plaque-forming units, is a way of counting how many infectious virus particles there are. We then kept the cells at 37 °C for 4 days, until the virus had completely damaged them. This damage is called cytopathic effect (CPE).

Next, we spun the cells and debris in a centrifuge at 2000× g for 10 min at 4 °C. A centrifuge spins samples very fast, so the cells pack together at the bottom as a small lump, or pellet. We mixed the pellets into culture medium without foetal bovine serum and broke them up with 10 strokes in a Dounce homogeniser, a glass tool for grinding cells. We then treated them with Vertel XF (Sigma), a chemical that frees virus particles from sticking to cell debris. This gave us a partly cleaned virus. We used it to infect KC cells at 0.05 pfu per cell, at 28 °C for 7 days. The virus in the liquid above the KC cells, 7 days after infection, was what we used to infect the mice.

2.4. How We Set Up the Experiment

We first compared the outer-coat proteins of all 27 types of the virus. For each type, we took a typical sequence of the building blocks (amino acids) of VP2 and of VP5. We lined these sequences up side by side using a program called ClustalX [36]. We then used a program called MegaX [37] to work out how the types are related, a bit like a family tree. This kind of analysis is called a phylogenetic analysis.

From the lined-up sequences, we built family trees using a method called maximum likelihood. It picks the tree that best explains the sequences we see. We used the Dayhoff substitution model, a set of rules for how often one building block tends to be swapped for another over time. We built the trees by swapping neighbouring branches step by step, a method called nearest-neighbour interchange. The groups of related VP2 or VP5 sequences helped us choose which virus proteins from BTV strains in different groups to vaccinate the IFNAR(−/−) mice with.

Each mouse was vaccinated twice, on day 0 and day 14. It received either 5 µg of rVP2 from BTV type 1, 4 or 8, or 5 µg of rVP5 from BTV-10. The proteins were mixed with Montanide ISA50V (SEPPIC), an adjuvant. An adjuvant is an ingredient that boosts the immune system's response to the protein. We used equal amounts of adjuvant and protein solution, a ratio of 1/1.

The rVP2 proteins of BTV-1 (accession number KP821004), BTV-4 (accession number KP821064) and BTV-8 (accession number KP821074) were made in Nicotiana benthamiana, a plant related to tobacco. We purified them as described in earlier papers [32,33]. The rVP5 protein of BTV-10 was also made in Nicotiana benthamiana and purified as described in an earlier paper [38].

We used 15 groups of IFNAR(−/−) mice, each with five mice aged 8–10 weeks (Table 1). Fourteen days after the second vaccination, we infected the mice with different BTV strains, as shown in Table 1. On the day of infection, each mouse was injected with 10³ pfu of live BTV. We watched all the mice for 14 days after infection.

To compare the qRT-PCR results between groups of mice, we used a statistical test called analysis of variance (ANOVA). It checks whether the average results of several groups differ by more than we would expect from normal variation. We followed it with Tukey's test (also called HSD, honestly significant difference), which compares the groups pair by pair. We called a difference statistically significant when p < 0.05, which matches a 95% confidence level. This means that if there were really no difference between the groups, a gap this large would appear by chance alone less than 5% of the time. The detailed results are given in Tables S3–S5.

2.5. Collecting Blood, Extracting RNA and Measuring the Virus with qRT-PCR

On days 0, 5, 7 and 12 after infection, we took about 50 µL of blood from each mouse. We drew it from the retro-orbital sinus, a blood-filled space behind the eye, and put it into tubes containing EDTA, a chemical that stops blood from clotting. We extracted RNA from these samples using TRIzol reagent (Thermo Fisher, les Ulis, France). RNA is the virus's genetic material, so measuring it tells us how much virus is in the blood.

In short, we added 20 µL of blood to 1 mL of TRIzol and shook it hard for 30 s. Then we added 200 µL of chloroform. We did each extraction twice. We shook the tubes for 30 s and left them on ice for 10 min so that the liquid separated into layers. We then spun the tubes in a centrifuge at 12,000× g for 10 min and collected the liquid on top. We cleaned the RNA from this liquid using the RNeasy minikit (Qiagen). We mixed the liquid with 350 µL of pure ethanol, put it onto the RNeasy column, and followed the maker's instructions for the rest. We washed the RNA off the column in 40 µL of RNase-free water, which is water free of enzymes that break down RNA. Finally, we ran the qRT-PCR as described earlier. We used primers, short pieces of genetic material that pick out the virus's genetic instructions, that were described before for BTV genome segment 10 [32,39,40,41].
parts.results:
3. Results

3.1. How the Virus Proteins Are Related, and How We Grouped the Mice

Of all the proteins in BTV, VP2 changes the most from one type of the virus to another [17]. We compared the VP2 proteins of the BTV types we chose for this study. To do this, we lined up their amino acid sequences. Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins, and the sequence is the order in which they are joined. We then worked out what percentage of the building blocks were the same in each pair of proteins.

Different strains of BTV-1 and BTV-8 shared only 52% to 54% of their VP2 building blocks. This placed them in separate clusters, called groups H and D (Figure 1). The VP2 proteins of these two types were even less alike to the VP2 of BTV-4, which they shared only 40% to 42% of their building blocks with. BTV-4 belongs to group A (Figure 1).

VP5 is the second most changeable of the BTV proteins [42]. Earlier studies compared VP5 proteins from different BTV types and found that they shared anywhere from 55.7% to 98.1% of their building blocks [39,43,44,45]. In our study, the mice were vaccinated with rVP5 from BTV-10. Here is how closely the VP5 proteins of the types we used match. VP5 from BTV-1 and rVP5 from BTV-10 share 78.3% of their building blocks. VP5 from BTV-4 and BTV-10 are 95.8% identical, and VP5 from BTV-8 and BTV-10 are 78.9% identical. Finally, VP5 from BTV-4 and BTV-8 are 79.5% identical. We chose the BTV strains partly so that they would include types that are only distantly related.

3.2. Signs of Illness in the Mice

Table S1 sums up the results of the vaccination and infection experiments in the IFNAR(−/−) mice. Figure 2, Figure 3 and Figure 4 show two things. The first is survival curves, which show how many mice were still alive as time went on. The second is the amount of BTV RNA in the blood, which tells us how much virus was present. We measured this with a test called real-time PCR, which we describe in Section 3.3.

Some mice were given the harmless salt solution (PBS) instead of a vaccine. We call these the comparison group, or mock-immunised group. When we infected them with BTV-4 or BTV-8 (Figure 2 and Figure 3), all of them developed signs of illness typical of a severe BTV infection (Table S2). These included watery eyes, scruffy hair and lying down unable to get up. All of these mice had died by day 5 after infection.

The comparison group infected with the weakened BTV-1 strain showed only mild signs of illness (Table S2), such as watery eyes and scruffy fur. They recovered fully and were still alive at the end of the experiment on day 14 after infection (Figure 4).

Next, we looked at mice vaccinated with rVP2 proteins from BTV-1, BTV-4 or BTV-8. When we infected them with the same type of virus, all of them were protected and showed no clear signs of illness. This was true for the mice infected with BTV-1 or BTV-4 (Table S1, groups 4 and 8, Figure 3 and Figure 4). Mice vaccinated with rVP2 from BTV-8 and then infected with BTV-8 (group 12, Figure 2) did develop very mild signs of illness on days 4 and 5 after infection. By day 7, they had recovered fully.

We also infected mice vaccinated with rVP2 from BTV-1, BTV-4 or BTV-8 with a different type of virus, either BTV-4 or BTV-8 (groups 9 and 11, Figure 2 and Figure 3). These mice showed no sign of protection. They developed severe signs of illness, much like the comparison group infected with the same viruses (groups 2 and 3).

The weakened BTV-1RGC7 strain gave a different result. Mice vaccinated with rVP2 from BTV-4 or BTV-8 and then infected with this weakened, different type (groups 7 and 10, Figure 4) developed more severe signs of illness than the comparison group infected with the same virus (group 1). All of them had died by day 5 after infection.

Mice vaccinated with VP5 from BTV-10 and then infected with BTV-4 or BTV-8 (groups 14 and 15, Figure 2 and Figure 3) also showed severe signs of illness. These were similar to those of the comparison groups infected with the same viruses (groups 2 and 3, Figure 2 and Figure 3), and all of these mice died on day 4 after infection.

When we infected mice vaccinated with rVP5 from BTV-10 with the weakened BTV-1RGC7 strain (group 13, Figure 4), all of them showed mild to severe signs of illness on day 5 after infection. The comparison group infected with the same virus did not do this. Instead, the illness in group 13 became much more severe, and all of these mice died on day 7 after infection. So the mice in this group survived slightly longer than the mice infected with the same BTV-1RGC7 virus after vaccination with rVP2 from BTV-4 or BTV-8 (groups 7 and 10).

3.3. Measuring BTV RNA in Mouse Blood with Real-Time PCR

To measure how much virus was in the blood, we used real-time PCR. This test copies the virus's genetic material, its RNA, over and over in repeated rounds. The more virus there is at the start, the sooner the copies build up to a level the machine can detect. The number of rounds needed is called the CT value. A lower CT value means more virus in the blood, and a higher CT value means less. Table S1 and Figure 2, Figure 3 and Figure 4 give the CT values.

The comparison groups had similar amounts of virus in their blood. On days 4 and 5 after infection with BTV-1RGC7, BTV-4 or BTV-8, their CT values ranged from 20.63 to 23.45, with averages of 22.11 to 22.7. The comparison mice infected with BTV-1RGC7 showed only mild signs of illness. This confirms that how severe the signs of illness are does not directly match how much virus is in the blood. Studies in cattle that vaccinated and then infected animals have reported the same thing [45].

Mice vaccinated with rVP2 were protected against the same type of virus they had been vaccinated with. Their average CT values were higher, meaning less virus in their blood. The average was 27.78 for BTV-1, 28.11 for BTV-4 and 28.6 for BTV-8. That is 5.6 to 6.2 CT values higher than in the matching comparison groups. This shows that vaccination with the matching protein significantly reduces the amount of virus in the blood after infection, by about 50 to 63 times. All of these protected mice survived to the end of the experiment on day 12 after infection, and they were humanely killed on day 14 after infection. Together with the milder signs of illness, this confirms that rVP2 could be a useful ingredient for vaccines made from separate protein pieces, each aimed at one type of the virus.

We also infected mice vaccinated with rVP2 from a different type of virus with the strong, disease-causing BTV-4 or BTV-8. These mice had CT values similar to, or 1 CT value higher than, those of the comparison groups. This points to little or no protection against other types of the virus, which we also saw when we compared signs of illness and deaths.

The weakened BTV-1RGC7 strain told a different story. When mice were vaccinated with rVP2 from BTV-4 or BTV-8 and then infected with BTV-1RGC7, their average CT values were lower by up to 2.7 CT values (Table S1, Figure 4). In other words, they had more virus in their blood. This rise in virus came with more severe signs of illness that killed the mice. It shows that BTV-1 multiplied more in mice that had been vaccinated with either of the two different rVP2 proteins. This points to a process like ADE.

Mice vaccinated with VP5 from BTV-10 and then infected with BTV-4 or BTV-8 had CT values, and severe signs of illness, similar to the comparison mice infected with the same viruses (Figure 2 and Figure 3). This shows that there was no significant protection.

However, when we infected mice vaccinated with VP5 from BTV-10 with BTV-1RGC7 (Figure 4), they had lower CT values on days 5 and 7 than the comparison mice infected with the same virus. Their CT values were 20.17 and 19.9, compared with averages of 22.7 and 28.1 in the comparison group on those days. These lower CT values, together with more severe signs of illness starting on day 3 after infection (Table S2), suggest that an ADE process involving the immune response to VP5 may be involved. It may be helping the weakened BTV-1RGC7 multiply and making the infection more severe.

We also compared the CT values of blood samples taken on days 4 and 5 after infection with BTV-1RGC7 (Figure 4, Table S1). We compared the comparison group (group 1), which had a mild infection, and the group vaccinated with VP2 from BTV-1 (group 4), which was protected. Both had CT values that were statistically significantly different from those of the groups vaccinated with VP2 from BTV-4 (group 7), VP2 from BTV-8 (group 10) or VP5 from BTV-10 (group 13). All of these groups had severe infections that killed the mice.

We call a difference statistically significant when, if there were really no difference between the groups, a gap this large would rarely appear by chance alone. Here, the gap was statistically significant at p < 0.05, which means less than 5% of the time. Table S5 gives the 95% confidence ranges, which show how precisely we could estimate each group's average.
parts.discussion:
4. Discussion

Earlier studies vaccinated sheep with virus-like particles (VLPs) made from BTV. These particles are tiny copies of the virus's outer shell, built in the lab using a baculovirus, a virus that infects insects. The sheep made high levels of neutralising antibodies, which stop the virus from infecting cells. They were also protected when they were later infected with the same type of virus they had been vaccinated with: BTV types 4, 10, 11, 13 and 17 [46]. This confirms that VLPs could be used as ingredients in vaccines.

There were also some signs of low levels of neutralising antibodies that worked against other types of the virus. The sheep were partly protected against these other types, meaning they had milder signs of illness. However, no evidence of ADE was found. The viruses in these studies had fairly closely related VP2 proteins. All of them belong to the same VP2 group, called VP2 group A [17] (Figure 1). This might help explain why the antibodies could still neutralise other types, even weakly.

In our earlier studies, we looked at how antibodies from the more distantly related BTV types 4 and 8 react with each other [17,33]. We vaccinated IFNAR(−/−) mice with VP2 proteins made in plants (rVP2). The mice made antibodies that recognised the same type of virus they had been vaccinated with. However, these antibodies neutralised the virus only weakly.

To measure this, we used a test called a microtiter assay. In this test, the blood serum is diluted step by step, and we find the dilution at which half of the virus is stopped. The result is called the neutralisation titre. The higher the titre, the more strongly the antibodies work. Our titres were only 2–3. This means the serum had to be diluted only a little before half of the virus was stopped. We also used a second test, called ELISA, which uses the rVP2 proteins as the target. In both tests, the reactions between the two types were too weak to detect.

Mice vaccinated with the rVP2 proteins were also protected when they were infected with strong, disease-causing strains of the same type of virus. However, these studies also suggested that ADE-type responses might happen. Mice vaccinated with rVP2 from one type could develop more severe signs of illness after infection with a different type.

In those earlier studies, the strong, disease-causing wild-type strains of BTV killed unprotected mice very quickly, within two to three days. This gave us only a short time to look for any ADE-type responses. Such responses could make the virus multiply more, make the illness more severe, or shorten survival even further after infection with a different type.

In the study we report here, we therefore used a weakened, harmless version of BTV-1RGC7 as the virus to infect the mice. We made this strain using reverse genetics, a method in which scientists read the virus's genetic code and rebuild the virus from it. We based it on the genetic code of the western reference strain of BTV-1 [35]. However, we do not yet know which genetic changes, or what process, make this strain weaker than the original BTV-1 reference strain.

We also used blood serum from rabbits that had been vaccinated with rVP2 from BTV-1, BTV-4 or BTV-8. In ELISA, all of these serums reacted very strongly with the matching protein [18]. The rabbit serum against rVP2 from BTV-8 also reacted weakly with the rVP2 proteins of both BTV-1 and BTV-4 [33]. The serum against rVP2 from BTV-4 reacted strongly with rVP2 from BTV-1, but not with rVP2 from BTV-8 [33]. The serum against rVP2 from BTV-1 reacted weakly with rVP2 from BTV-4, and again did not react with rVP2 from BTV-8 [33].

We also tested these rabbit serums against blood serum from sheep that had been infected with the matching type of virus. In each case, the rVP2 proteins of the three types reacted strongly with the sheep serum. However, the only reaction between the BTV-8 serum and the rVP2 protein of BTV-4 was very weak [33].

The rabbit serums against BTV rVP2 proteins, and the sheep serums from infected animals against BTV-1, BTV-4 and BTV-8, all contained neutralising antibodies against the matching type. None of them neutralised either of the other types used in this study [33].

To measure how much virus was in the blood, we used the qRT-PCR test. This test gives a number called the CT value. The lower the CT value, the more virus RNA is in the blood. In our study, the lowest CT values, meaning the most virus in the blood, were in mice infected with BTV-1RGC7 after vaccination with rVP2 from BTV-8 or rVP2 from BTV-4. This suggests that one or more ADE processes may help this weakened BTV-1 infect the mice.

We do not know what this is linked to. It could be related to the way BTV-1RGC7 is weakened, which has not yet been worked out, and to the weakened virus becoming able to cause disease again. Or it could reflect how the VP2 proteins of the different BTV strains involved react with each other.

Earlier studies have ruled out VP5 as a target for neutralising antibodies [23,28]. However, VP5 can help to tell one type of the virus from another [21,22,39]. It may do this by limiting the shapes that VP2 can take. Mice vaccinated with rVP5 from BTV-10 and then infected with the weakened BTV-1 also showed signs of more infection. This suggests that ADE of infection and illness is not limited to antibodies that attach to VP2. It could also be caused by any non-neutralising antibodies that attach to the outer coat of BTV.

However, in our study these effects were limited to BTV-1. Earlier vaccination studies in calves found the same pattern: calves vaccinated against BTV-8 and then infected with BTV-9 [10]. Together, these results suggest that the kind of response may vary. It may depend on which type the antibodies recognise and which strain infects the animal.

BTV virus particles can attach to antibodies that are already in the body but do not neutralise the virus. This may help the virus be recognised and taken up by dendritic macrophages [11]. These are immune cells that pick up germs and show pieces of them to other immune cells. This could happen in the early stages of infection. It could make the virus spread faster through the infected animal, before the animal makes its own neutralising antibodies against that type.

If the virus spreads early, it could multiply more overall and cause more damage to the body's tissues. BTV particles bound to existing antibodies could also lead to more cytokines being released and to more death of endothelial cells, the cells that line the blood vessels [10,11]. Cytokines are chemical signals that immune cells use to communicate. This could make the signs of illness more severe.

IFNAR(−/−) mice have been used before as a model to study the protection given by experimental orbivirus vaccines or by possible antiviral molecules [32,39,47,48,49,50,51]. Earlier studies found protection across different types after animals were vaccinated with live, weakened BTV vaccines one after another, or infected with several types of the virus [52]. This protection may depend more on protective T-cell responses that work across different types. Such responses have been shown to target BTV proteins that are not part of the outer coat [2]. It may depend less on neutralising antibodies that work across types. However, we cannot rule out low levels of cross-neutralisation between strains whose VP2 proteins are closely related [33].

Vaccinating sheep with virus-like particles made from baculovirus, representing different types of BTV, suggested that there might be a low level of cross-neutralisation. This would likely hide any ADE-like effects. However, the types tested in those earlier studies had fairly closely related VP2 proteins, all belonging to VP2 group A [17].

The severity of signs of illness seen after BTV vaccination and infection seems likely to come from a mix of antibody responses and T-cell responses. This mix differs from one animal to another. It depends on how the different BTV strains are related and on the animal's past vaccinations or infections.
